lessons.title: The Shape of a Federal Civil Case
body: Civil procedure is the body of rules that governs how a private dispute is brought, tried and ended, as opposed to substantive law, which says who is entitled to what. A contract rule tells you whether a promise is enforceable; civil procedure tells you which court may hear the claim, how the defendant is told about it, what must be pleaded, what each side may learn from the other, and when the case is over. A great deal of litigation is lost on procedure before anyone reaches the merits.

Federal courts are courts of limited jurisdiction. They have only the power that Article III of the Constitution permits and that Congress has actually granted by statute. The Supreme Court has said that a federal court presumes it lacks jurisdiction and that the party invoking it bears the burden of showing it exists, in Kokkonen v. Guardian Life Insurance Co. of America (1994). State trial courts, by contrast, are generally courts of general jurisdiction and can hear almost anything unless a law takes it away. The practical consequence is that a federal plaintiff must always plead a basis for subject-matter jurisdiction, and a federal judge must check it even if no party raises it. A court must establish jurisdiction before it decides the merits, a rule reinforced in Steel Co. v. Citizens for a Better Environment (1998).

The Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, first adopted in 1938, govern procedure in the district courts. Congress authorised the Supreme Court to prescribe them in the Rules Enabling Act, 28 U.S.C. section 2072, provided that they are general rules of practice and procedure that do not abridge, enlarge or modify any substantive right. That limit becomes important in the Erie doctrine. Rule 1 says the rules should be construed to secure the just, speedy and inexpensive determination of every action. Under Rule 3 a civil action is commenced by filing a complaint with the court.

The typical case has recognisable stages. The plaintiff files a complaint and serves it with a summons. The defendant responds either by a motion under Rule 12, attacking the complaint without admitting anything, or by an answer. The parties exchange information in discovery. Either side may move for summary judgment, which ends the case if no genuine factual dispute exists. If not, there is a trial, a judgment, post-trial motions and an appeal. Each later lesson in this course sits at one of those stages.

Worked example. Dana, a resident of Ohio, sues a neighbour in the same town in federal court for negligently flooding her garden, pleading only state tort law. The court has no basis to hear the case: there is no federal question and no diversity of citizenship. Even if the neighbour never objects and both sides spend a year in discovery, the court must dismiss when the defect is noticed, because the parties cannot create subject-matter jurisdiction by consent or silence.

lessons.title: Federal Question Jurisdiction
body: Federal question jurisdiction is conferred by 28 U.S.C. section 1331, which gives district courts original jurisdiction over civil actions arising under the Constitution, laws or treaties of the United States. The Constitution allows much broader federal-question power than Congress has granted in section 1331, so the statutory test, not the constitutional one, is what usually controls.

The ordinary test is that a case arises under federal law when federal law creates the cause of action asserted. Most federal question cases are of this kind: a claim under the federal civil rights statutes, the securities laws, or the patent laws. The jurisdictional question is answered from the face of the plaintiff's complaint under the well-pleaded complaint rule, which comes from Louisville and Nashville Railroad Co. v. Mottley (1908). In that case a couple sued a railroad for breach of a contract that gave them lifetime passes, and they anticipated that the railroad would defend by invoking a federal statute that, the railroad said, barred free passes. The Court held there was no federal jurisdiction, because a plaintiff's own complaint must present the federal issue, and an anticipated federal defence does not count. It follows that a federal defence, and even a federal counterclaim, cannot by itself be the basis for jurisdiction or for removal.

There is a narrow second route. A state-law claim can arise under federal law if it necessarily raises a federal issue that is actually disputed and substantial, and that a federal court may entertain without disturbing the congressionally approved balance of federal and state judicial responsibilities. This is the test of Grable and Sons Metal Products, Inc. v. Darue Engineering and Manufacturing (2005), where a quiet-title action turned on whether the Internal Revenue Service had given proper notice under a federal statute. Gunn v. Minton (2013) applied the test strictly and held that a state-law legal malpractice claim arising from a lost patent case did not qualify, because the federal patent question would not change the real-world result of the patent case and was not important to the federal system as a whole. Earlier, Merrell Dow Pharmaceuticals Inc. v. Thompson (1986) refused jurisdiction where a state tort claim mentioned a federal statute that gave no private right of action.

Worked example. Lena sues Harbor Bank in state court for breach of a loan agreement. She alleges only state contract law. Harbor Bank intends to argue that a federal banking statute preempts her claim. Harbor Bank may not remove the case to federal court on that ground, because the federal issue appears only in the anticipated defence. If Lena had instead sued under a federal consumer-protection statute that creates a private right of action, the case would arise under federal law and the defendant could remove it.

lessons.title: Diversity Jurisdiction
body: Diversity jurisdiction lets a federal court hear state-law claims between citizens of different states, on the theory that an out-of-state litigant might fear bias in a local court. Under 28 U.S.C. section 1332(a), the district courts have original jurisdiction over civil actions where the matter in controversy exceeds $75,000, exclusive of interest and costs, and the dispute is between citizens of different states, or between citizens of a state and citizens or subjects of a foreign state. Two requirements follow: diversity of citizenship and the amount in controversy.

Since Strawbridge v. Curtiss (1806), the statute has been read to require complete diversity: no plaintiff may be a citizen of the same state as any defendant. If one plaintiff and one defendant share citizenship, the whole case fails the test as pleaded. Citizenship is measured when the complaint is filed. For a natural person, citizenship means domicile, which is physical presence in a state combined with an intent to remain indefinitely; residence alone is not enough. A corporation is a citizen of every state where it is incorporated and of the state where it has its principal place of business. In Hertz Corp. v. Friend (2010), the Court defined that place as the corporation's nerve center, normally its headquarters where officers direct and control its activities, not merely the place with the most operations. Unincorporated associations such as partnerships are citizens of every state of which any member is a citizen, following Carden v. Arkoma Associates (1990), and the courts of appeals apply the same member-by-member rule to limited liability companies. A United States citizen domiciled abroad is treated as neither a state citizen nor an alien and so cannot be sued or sue in diversity, as shown in Newman-Green, Inc. v. Alfonzo-Larrain (1989).

The amount in controversy is measured by what the plaintiff claims in good faith, and the claim controls unless it appears to a legal certainty that the plaintiff cannot recover more than the threshold, the test from St. Paul Mercury Indemnity Co. v. Red Cab Co. (1938). A single plaintiff may aggregate all claims, related or not, against a single defendant. Separate plaintiffs generally cannot add their claims together, though supplemental jurisdiction can change the result, as the next lesson explains. Federal courts also decline to hear domestic-relations and probate matters even when diversity exists, under Ankenbrandt v. Richards (1992).

Worked example. Priya, domiciled in Texas, sues Orion Corp. and Marcus for $200,000 in contract damages. Orion is incorporated in Delaware with headquarters in Texas. Orion is a citizen of both Delaware and Texas, so Priya shares citizenship with it, and diversity is lacking. Dropping Orion would not help if Orion is an indispensable party; the plaintiff must restructure the case or file in state court.

lessons.title: Supplemental Jurisdiction and Removal
body: Supplemental jurisdiction lets a federal court hear a claim that has no independent jurisdictional basis because it is attached to a claim that does. It is codified in 28 U.S.C. section 1367(a), which extends jurisdiction to all claims in the same case or controversy under Article III. The leading pre-statute case, United Mine Workers v. Gibbs (1966), said that claims form one case if they derive from a common nucleus of operative fact, such that a plaintiff would ordinarily be expected to try them all in one proceeding. So a plaintiff who sues under federal law for firing in violation of a federal statute may add a state-law wrongful-discharge claim arising from the same firing.

Section 1367(b) limits the power in diversity cases to prevent plaintiffs from using it to sidestep complete diversity. Where jurisdiction rests only on section 1332, courts may not hear claims by plaintiffs against persons made parties under Rules 14, 19, 20 or 24, or claims by persons proposed to be joined as plaintiffs under Rule 19 or seeking to intervene under Rule 24, when doing so would be inconsistent with section 1332. Defendants' claims, such as a compulsory counterclaim or a third-party claim by a defendant, face no such limit. Owen Equipment and Erection Co. v. Kroger (1978) is the standard illustration: a plaintiff who sued a diverse defendant could not assert a claim against a non-diverse third-party defendant who was brought in by the defendant. Under section 1367(c), the court may decline supplemental jurisdiction where the claim raises a novel state issue, substantially predominates, or the court has dismissed all claims over which it had original jurisdiction. Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Allapattah Services, Inc. (2005) held that, once complete diversity exists, section 1367 permits jurisdiction over additional plaintiffs whose claims are below the amount in controversy, so long as at least one plaintiff meets it.

Removal is the defendant's power to move a case from state to federal court. Under section 1441(a), a civil action brought in state court may be removed if the federal court would have had original jurisdiction, and removal goes to the federal district embracing the state court's location. In diversity cases a defendant who is a citizen of the forum state may not remove, the forum-defendant rule of section 1441(b)(2). All properly joined and served defendants must consent. Under section 1446(b), the notice of removal is due within 30 days after the defendant receives the initial pleading or service, and a diversity case generally may not be removed more than one year after commencement absent bad faith. A case removed without jurisdiction is remanded under section 1447(c), and a lack of subject-matter jurisdiction may be raised at any time before final judgment.

Worked example. Chen, a Florida citizen, sues a Georgia citizen in a Georgia state court for $500,000 on a state-law claim. Although the parties are completely diverse and the amount exceeds $75,000, the defendant is a citizen of the forum state, so the forum-defendant rule bars removal and the case stays in state court. If Chen had sued the same defendant in a Florida state court, the defendant could remove within 30 days of service.

lessons.title: Personal Jurisdiction: From Pennoyer to International Shoe
body: Personal jurisdiction is a court's power over the defendant as a person, as distinct from subject-matter jurisdiction, which is the power over the type of case. It is a requirement of due process: in state court it flows from the Fourteenth Amendment, and for exercises of federal power it flows from the Fifth Amendment. Unlike subject-matter jurisdiction, personal jurisdiction is a personal right that a defendant can waive, by failing to raise it in the first Rule 12 motion or responsive pleading under Rule 12(h)(1), or by consenting.

In Pennoyer v. Neff (1878), the Court tied jurisdiction to physical power: a state could bind persons found within its borders and property located there, and could not reach nonresidents through service outside its territory. That rigid view collapsed in the age of corporations and automobiles. International Shoe Co. v. Washington (1945) replaced it. A court may exercise jurisdiction over an absent defendant if the defendant has certain minimum contacts with the forum such that the suit does not offend traditional notions of fair play and substantial justice. In the case, a Delaware corporation based in Missouri with salesmen operating in Washington was held subject to suit in Washington to collect unemployment contributions, since the claims arose out of its activities there. The opinion distinguished claims arising from the defendant's forum activities from unrelated claims, a split that later became the line between specific and general jurisdiction.

Pennoyer's territorial bases survive in modified form. Burnham v. Superior Court (1990) held that a state may exercise jurisdiction over a nonresident personally served with process while voluntarily present in the state, even briefly and even on an unrelated matter, so-called tag jurisdiction. All nine Justices agreed on the result but split on the reasoning: a plurality relied on the historical pedigree of in-state service, while four Justices asked whether the defendant had purposefully availed himself of the forum's benefits. Domicile in the state, consent, and appearance also support jurisdiction. Rule 4(k)(1)(A) incorporates state law: a federal district court may exercise jurisdiction over any defendant who would be subject to the jurisdiction of a court of general jurisdiction in the state where the federal court sits, which usually means the limits of the state's long-arm statute and of due process.

Worked example. Sam, a resident of Oregon, is served with a summons in a business dispute while changing planes in an Illinois airport. Under Burnham he is subject to personal jurisdiction in Illinois courts, though the court may later transfer the case on convenience grounds, and Sam may argue that fraud or force lured him there. If instead the summons was mailed to Oregon, Illinois would have to find minimum contacts.

lessons.title: Specific Jurisdiction
body: Specific jurisdiction exists when the claim arises out of or relates to the defendant's contacts with the forum. Courts ask three questions in order. First, did the defendant purposefully avail itself of the privilege of conducting activities in the forum, or purposefully direct its conduct there? Second, does the claim arise out of or relate to those contacts? Third, would exercising jurisdiction be reasonable under factors such as the burden on the defendant, the forum's interest, the plaintiff's interest and the interstate judicial system's interest? The defendant's contacts must be its own choice, not the unilateral activity of the plaintiff or a third party, as Burger King Corp. v. Rudzewicz (1985) and Walden v. Fiore (2014) stress. Walden holds that the relevant contacts are those the defendant creates with the forum state itself, not contacts with persons who happen to reside there.

World-Wide Volkswagen Corp. v. Woodson (1980) is the classic limit. A New York couple's Audi caught fire in Oklahoma; the Oklahoma courts could not reach the New York dealer and regional distributor, because the foreseeability that matters is not that a product may travel but that the defendant should reasonably anticipate being haled into court in the forum. Where a manufacturer places goods into a stream of commerce, the Court has not agreed on a rule. In Asahi Metal Industry Co. v. Superior Court (1987), the opinions split between a view requiring something more than awareness that goods would reach the forum and a view that awareness suffices, but a majority agreed that jurisdiction would be unreasonable in that indemnification dispute between foreign companies. J. McIntyre Machinery, Ltd. v. Nicastro (2011) produced a plurality that rejected jurisdiction over an English manufacturer whose machine injured a worker in New Jersey, with two concurring Justices resting on narrower grounds.

Two more cases mark the edges. Calder v. Jones (1984) allowed jurisdiction in California over Florida writers whose article about a California resident was aimed at California and caused harm there. Bristol-Myers Squibb Co. v. Superior Court (2017) held that California courts lacked specific jurisdiction over claims by nonresidents who were not prescribed or injured by the drug in California, even though other plaintiffs from California had similar claims. Ford Motor Co. v. Montana Eighth Judicial District Court (2021) held that the phrase arise out of or relate to does not demand strict causation: Ford served the market for its vehicles in Montana and Minnesota, so in-state accidents involving those models fell within specific jurisdiction.

Worked example. A Utah company sells software online only to businesses and never targets Maine. A Maine plaintiff buys it by chance. Jurisdiction in Maine is doubtful because the sale was the plaintiff's unilateral contact. If the company had advertised in Maine and shipped there regularly, a Maine court could hear a claim arising from those sales.

lessons.title: General Jurisdiction and Consent
body: General jurisdiction, also called all-purpose jurisdiction, lets a court hear any claim against a defendant, even one unrelated to the forum, because the defendant is essentially at home there. The modern test is narrow. Goodyear Dunlop Tires Operations, S.A. v. Brown (2011) held that foreign subsidiaries of an American tire manufacturer, whose tires reached North Carolina only through others, were not at home there, even though the tires were sold in the state. Daimler AG v. Bauman (2014) rejected an agency theory under which a subsidiary's in-state contacts would be attributed to the foreign parent, and said that for corporations the paradigm forums are the place of incorporation and the principal place of business, with only an exceptional case supporting more. For individuals, the paradigm forum is domicile.

The Court applied the same view in BNSF Railway Co. v. Tyrrell (2017), where a railroad with substantial track and employees in Montana was not at home there, so Montana courts could not hear a claim by non-residents for injuries elsewhere. The test thus avoids a result in which a large company is at home everywhere it does heavy business. A company may have several homes, but not every state where it earns revenue.

Consent is a separate basis. A defendant may agree in a contract to be sued in a particular forum, and forum-selection clauses are generally enforced. A defendant waives an objection by failing to raise personal jurisdiction in the first Rule 12 response. In Mallory v. Norfolk Southern Railway Co. (2023), the Court, by a closely divided vote, held that due process does not bar a state from requiring an out-of-state corporation to consent to personal jurisdiction as a condition of registering to do business there, as Pennsylvania's statute did. The decision rested on an older precedent, Pennsylvania Fire Insurance Co. v. Gold Issue Mining Co. (1917), and left open questions about other limits such as the dormant Commerce Clause.

Notice is a distinct due process requirement. Under Mullane v. Central Hanover Bank and Trust Co. (1950), notice must be reasonably calculated, under all the circumstances, to apprise interested parties of the action and give them a chance to object. Publication alone fails when an address is known.

Worked example. Brightline Foods, incorporated in Delaware with headquarters in Georgia, is sued in California by a Californian for a defective product that the plaintiff bought in Nevada. California has no specific jurisdiction because the claim is unrelated to California, and Brightline is not at home there, so general jurisdiction fails unless Brightline consented, for example through a registration statute that treats registration as consent.

lessons.title: Venue, Transfer and Forum Non Conveniens
body: Venue is a statutory rule about which court within a system is the proper place for a case. It exists for convenience and is not jurisdictional. Under 28 U.S.C. section 1391(b), a civil action may be brought in a district where any defendant resides, if all defendants are residents of the state in which the district sits; a district where a substantial part of the events or omissions giving rise to the claim occurred; or, if no district qualifies under those two rules, any district where any defendant is subject to the court's personal jurisdiction. Under section 1391(c), a natural person resides where he is domiciled, and an entity defendant resides in any district where it is subject to personal jurisdiction in the action in question. Objection to venue is made under Rule 12(b)(3) and is waived if omitted from the first Rule 12 response.

A properly venued case can still be moved. Under 28 U.S.C. section 1404(a), for the convenience of parties and witnesses and in the interest of justice, a court may transfer a civil action to any other district where it might have been brought or to which all parties have consented. The court weighs private factors such as evidence and witness access and public factors such as docket congestion and local interest. In Van Dusen v. Barrack (1964), the Court held that a transfer on the defendant's motion carries the transferor state's law with it, so transfer does not change the choice-of-law rules, and Ferens v. John Deere Co. (1990) extended this to transfer sought by the plaintiff. Atlantic Marine Construction Co. v. United States District Court (2013) held that a valid forum-selection clause should be enforced through section 1404(a) with the plaintiff's choice receiving no weight, and that the transferor state's choice-of-law rules do not follow a transfer made because of such a clause.

Where venue is wrong, section 1406(a) requires dismissal or, in the interest of justice, transfer. Goldlawr, Inc. v. Heiman (1962) permits transfer under section 1406 even if the transferor court lacks personal jurisdiction over the defendant. Where the better forum is a court outside the federal system, such as a foreign court or a state court, the tool is the common-law doctrine of forum non conveniens, applied in Gulf Oil Corp. v. Gilbert (1947) and Piper Aircraft Co. v. Reyno (1981). The court asks whether an adequate alternative forum exists and then balances private and public interests. Piper held that a less favourable change in law in the alternative forum does not by itself make it inadequate. Sinochem International Co. v. Malaysia International Shipping Corp. (2007) allows a court to dismiss on this ground without first deciding jurisdiction.

Worked example. A Colorado plaintiff sues an Arizona company in Colorado for a contract signed in Arizona and performed there. If the company is subject to jurisdiction in Colorado but the events occurred in Arizona, a Colorado venue may be improper under section 1391(b)(2), and the court can transfer to Arizona under section 1406.

lessons.title: Notice, Service of Process and Timing
body: Service of process is the formal delivery of the summons and complaint. It serves two functions: it gives constitutionally adequate notice, measured by the Mullane standard, and it is the procedural step by which the court asserts authority over the defendant. Even a defendant with actual knowledge of a suit may defeat jurisdiction if service was not made as the rules require, although courts often allow plaintiffs to cure defects.

Rule 4 governs. Under Rule 4(c)(2), anyone who is at least 18 years old and not a party may serve the summons and complaint. Under Rule 4(e), an individual in the United States may be served by following the state law of the state where the court sits or where service is made, by delivering a copy personally, by leaving a copy at the individual's dwelling with someone of suitable age and discretion who resides there, or by delivering to an authorised agent. Rule 4(h) provides comparable methods for corporations, including delivery to an officer, a managing or general agent, or an agent authorised by appointment or law. Rule 4(d) creates a waiver system: the plaintiff may mail a request for waiver, and a defendant who returns the waiver avoids the formalities and gets extra time, generally 60 days from when the request was sent to respond rather than 21 days. A defendant who unjustifiably refuses to waive may be charged the costs of formal service.

Time limits matter. Under Rule 4(m), if the defendant is not served within 90 days after the complaint is filed, the court must dismiss without prejudice or order that service be made within a specified time, and must extend the time if the plaintiff shows good cause. Courts also have discretion to extend without good cause. Under Rule 12(a)(1)(A)(i), a defendant has 21 days after being served to answer. A defendant who fails to respond risks default under Rule 55, although the court can set aside an entry of default for good cause. Defects in service are raised through Rule 12(b)(4), for insufficient process, and Rule 12(b)(5), for insufficient service of process, and are waived if omitted from the first Rule 12 motion or responsive pleading.

Service does not itself create personal jurisdiction. Rule 4(k) states when service establishes it: it does so for defendants subject to the jurisdiction of the state court where the federal court sits, as well as where a federal statute authorises nationwide service or, under Rule 4(k)(2), for claims arising under federal law against a defendant who is not subject to jurisdiction in any state but has sufficient contacts with the United States as a whole.

Worked example. A process server leaves the papers with a roommate at Alex's apartment. If the roommate is an adult residing there, service meets Rule 4(e)(2)(B). If it is a visiting friend who lives elsewhere, service is defective, and Alex should raise it in a first Rule 12 motion or lose the objection.

lessons.title: The Erie Doctrine
body: A federal court hearing a state-law claim under diversity or supplemental jurisdiction has to decide which law supplies the rule of decision. For nearly a century the answer was uncertain. Swift v. Tyson (1842) allowed federal courts to apply their own general common law in diversity cases. Erie Railroad Co. v. Tompkins (1938) overruled it. Justice Brandeis wrote that there is no federal general common law, and that, in matters not governed by federal statute or the Constitution, a federal court sitting in diversity applies state substantive law, including state court decisions. The reasoning was constitutional and practical: Swift allowed forum shopping between state and federal courts and produced inequitable administration of the laws.

Erie did not eliminate federal procedure. The hard cases concern whether a given rule is substantive, so that state law governs, or procedural, so that federal law governs. The cases follow a pattern. Guaranty Trust Co. v. York (1945) asked whether applying federal law would be outcome determinative, in the sense that it would substantially affect the result, which proved too broad. Byrd v. Blue Ridge Rural Electric Cooperative (1958) recognised that countervailing federal interests, there the federal tradition of jury trial, could outweigh a state rule. Hanna v. Plumer (1965) supplies the modern framework. If a valid Federal Rule of Civil Procedure directly covers the point in dispute, the court applies the Rule, as long as it is within the Rules Enabling Act and the Constitution. If there is no controlling Federal Rule and the issue is a judge-made or statutory federal practice, the court applies the twin aims of Erie: discouraging forum shopping and avoiding inequitable administration of the laws.

Application has been contested. Walker v. Armco Steel Corp. (1980) held that Rule 3, which says an action commences by filing a complaint, does not displace a state rule that an action commences for limitations purposes only on service, because Rule 3 was not meant to toll state limitations. Shady Grove Orthopedic Associates v. Allstate Insurance Co. (2010) held that Rule 23 governed whether a class action could proceed in federal court and displaced a New York law barring class actions for statutory penalties, though the Justices divided on the reasoning, with Justice Stevens concurring on narrower grounds. Gasperini v. Center for Humanities, Inc. (1996) required federal courts to apply the state standard for excessive jury awards while keeping judge-jury allocation under federal practice.

Two related points matter. Klaxon Co. v. Stentor Electric Manufacturing Co. (1941) requires the federal court to apply the choice-of-law rules of the state in which it sits. And when the state's highest court has not decided an issue, the federal court predicts how it would rule, treating decisions of intermediate state appellate courts as persuasive evidence.

Worked example. A federal court in Ohio hears a diversity negligence claim. Ohio law sets the statute of limitations, and whether a limitations period is tolled is also state law. But whether the plaintiff may amend the complaint is governed by Rule 15, because a Federal Rule directly covers it.

lessons.title: Pleading: Twombly and Iqbal
body: Rule 8(a)(2) requires a complaint to contain a short and plain statement of the claim showing that the pleader is entitled to relief. Rule 8(a)(1) requires a short statement of the grounds for jurisdiction, and Rule 8(a)(3) a demand for the relief sought. A defendant may move to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6) for failure to state a claim upon which relief can be granted. The court tests only the sufficiency of the pleading, taking factual allegations as true and drawing reasonable inferences for the plaintiff. It does not weigh evidence.

For decades, Conley v. Gibson (1957) was understood to say that a complaint should not be dismissed unless it appears beyond doubt that the plaintiff can prove no set of facts entitling him to relief. Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly (2007) retired that language. In an antitrust conspiracy case, the Court held that a plaintiff must plead enough facts to state a claim that is plausible on its face. Allegations of parallel conduct by competitors were consistent with both conspiracy and lawful independent behaviour, so they did not nudge the claim across the line from conceivable to plausible. Ashcroft v. Iqbal (2009) confirmed that the plausibility standard applies to all civil actions. It described a two-step approach: first, a court sets aside legal conclusions and formulaic recitals, which are not entitled to the presumption of truth; second, it assumes the truth of well-pleaded facts and decides whether they plausibly give rise to an entitlement to relief, a context-specific task drawing on judicial experience and common sense. The case concerned allegations that senior officials had adopted a discriminatory detention policy, and the Court found the allegations insufficient as to those defendants.

Some boundaries should be learned. Rule 9(b) requires fraud and mistake to be pleaded with particularity, though malice, intent and knowledge may be alleged generally. Swierkiewicz v. Sorema N.A. (2002) held that an employment discrimination complaint need not plead facts establishing the elements of a prima facie case. Erickson v. Pardus (2007) reaffirms that pro se pleadings are construed liberally. Johnson v. City of Shelby (2014) holds that a complaint need not cite the correct legal theory. Rule 8(d) allows alternative and even inconsistent pleading.

Rule 11 operates beside pleading doctrine. By signing a filing, a lawyer certifies after reasonable inquiry that legal contentions are warranted and factual contentions have or are likely to have evidentiary support. A party served with a Rule 11 motion has 21 days to withdraw the challenged paper before the motion may be filed, the safe-harbour provision.

Worked example. A plaintiff alleges only that two competing airlines raised fares on the same day and that therefore they must have agreed. After Twombly, the court would likely dismiss because parallel pricing in an industry is as consistent with independent decisions as with agreement. If she also alleged a recorded call in which executives fixed the new prices, the complaint would survive.

lessons.title: Responses, Amendment and Default
body: A defendant's first response is either an answer or a pre-answer motion. Rule 12(b) lists seven defences that may be raised by motion: lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, lack of personal jurisdiction, improper venue, insufficient process, insufficient service of process, failure to state a claim, and failure to join a party under Rule 19. Rule 12(g)(2) generally forbids a second Rule 12 motion raising a defence that was available but omitted from the first. Rule 12(h)(1) provides that defences of personal jurisdiction, venue, process and service are waived if they are not included in the first Rule 12 motion or, if no motion is made, in the answer or an amendment allowed as of right. By contrast, subject-matter jurisdiction may be raised at any time, and failure to state a claim, failure to join a required party and the merits defence may be raised later in the pleadings, by a Rule 12(c) motion or at trial.

An answer must admit or deny each allegation under Rule 8(b); allegations not denied are treated as admitted, except those about damages. Rule 8(c) lists affirmative defences, such as the statute of limitations, release and res judicata, which must be pleaded or are waived. Rule 13(a) makes a counterclaim compulsory if it arises out of the same transaction or occurrence as the opposing party's claim, and a compulsory counterclaim not pleaded is lost; Rule 13(b) allows other counterclaims as permissive, and Rule 13(g) permits crossclaims against coparties.

Amendment is liberally allowed. Under Rule 15(a)(1), a party may amend once as a matter of course within 21 days after serving it or within 21 days after service of a responsive pleading or a Rule 12(b), (e) or (f) motion, whichever is later. Afterwards a party needs the opposing party's consent or the court's leave, and the court should give leave freely when justice so requires. Rule 15(c) governs relation back for limitations: an amendment relates back when the law providing the limitations period allows it or when the amendment asserts a claim arising out of the same conduct, transaction or occurrence as the original pleading. An amendment changing the party against whom the claim is asserted relates back if, within the period for service under Rule 4(m), the new party received notice and knew or should have known that, but for a mistake about identity, the action would have been brought against it. Krupski v. Costa Crociere S.p.A. (2010) held that the inquiry focuses on what the party to be added knew or should have known, not on the plaintiff's own diligence.

If a defendant fails to plead or defend, the clerk enters default under Rule 55(a), and a default judgment follows under Rule 55(b). A court may set aside an entry of default for good cause, and a final default judgment may be set aside under Rule 60(b).

Worked example. Nadia is sued and files a Rule 12(b)(6) motion only. Months later she tries to argue lack of personal jurisdiction. Under Rule 12(g)(2) and (h)(1) the objection is waived, because she omitted it from her first Rule 12 motion.

lessons.title: Joinder of Claims and Parties
body: Joinder rules decide who and what may be put into one lawsuit. Rule 18(a) allows a party asserting a claim to join as many claims as it has against an opposing party, related or not. That is broad, but each claim still needs its own basis for subject-matter jurisdiction, subject to supplemental jurisdiction and aggregation of amount in controversy against a single defendant.

Party joinder is more restricted. Rule 20(a) permits plaintiffs to join if they assert a right to relief arising out of the same transaction, occurrence or series of transactions or occurrences, and if any question of law or fact common to all plaintiffs will arise. The same test applies to defendants. Rule 21 provides that misjoinder is not a ground for dismissing an action, and the court may add or drop parties.

Rule 19 addresses persons whom the action cannot fairly proceed without. A person must be joined if feasible when the court cannot give complete relief among existing parties without them, or when the person claims an interest in the subject of the action and disposing of it in their absence would impair their ability to protect it or leave an existing party exposed to a substantial risk of double or inconsistent obligations. If a required person cannot be joined because it would destroy diversity or venue, or the person is not subject to personal jurisdiction, the court decides under Rule 19(b) whether in equity and good conscience the action should proceed or be dismissed, weighing prejudice, the ability to shape relief, adequacy of a judgment in their absence, and whether the plaintiff has an alternative forum. Temple v. Synthes Corp. (1990) held that joint tortfeasors are not required parties, only permissive ones, because each is jointly and severally liable. Republic of Philippines v. Pimentel (2008) shows a case where an absent sovereign with immunity made dismissal proper.

Rule 14 impleader allows a defending party to bring in a nonparty who is or may be liable to it for all or part of the claim against it. A defendant need not seek leave if it files the third-party complaint within 14 days after serving its original answer. Impleader is for derivative liability such as indemnity or contribution; a defendant cannot implead someone merely because they are also responsible to the plaintiff. Rule 22 interpleader allows a stakeholder who faces multiple claims to the same property to require the claimants to litigate among themselves. Statutory interpleader under 28 U.S.C. section 1335 requires only minimal diversity among claimants and at least $500 at stake, while Rule 22 interpleader needs ordinary jurisdiction, including complete diversity between the stakeholder and the claimants. Rule 24 allows intervention of right, when the applicant claims an interest that may be impaired and is not adequately represented, and permissive intervention when the applicant has a claim sharing a common question.

Worked example. Marta sues a trucking company after a crash. The company wants to bring in its insurer, who has a contractual duty to cover the loss. Impleader under Rule 14 is available because the insurer may be liable to the company. Marta's own claim against a non-diverse driver cannot be added through section 1367 if it would defeat diversity under section 1367(b).

lessons.title: Class Actions
body: A class action lets one or more named plaintiffs sue on behalf of a large group whose members have similar claims. It exists because small individual claims are often not worth litigating alone, and because separate suits would waste resources or risk inconsistent results. The price is that absent class members may be bound by a judgment without having participated.

Rule 23(a) sets four prerequisites that every class must meet: numerosity, so that joinder is impracticable; commonality, meaning questions of law or fact common to the class; typicality of the representatives' claims or defences; and adequacy, meaning the representatives and their counsel will fairly and adequately protect the class. Rule 23(b) then requires one of three types. Rule 23(b)(1) covers risks of inconsistent adjudications or impairment of other members' interests, as in a limited fund. Rule 23(b)(2) applies where the defendant has acted on grounds applying generally to the class, so that final injunctive or declaratory relief is appropriate for the whole class. Rule 23(b)(3) covers damages classes where common questions predominate over individual ones and a class action is superior to other methods. For (b)(3) classes, members must receive the best notice practicable and a right to opt out under Rule 23(c)(2)(B).

Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. v. Dukes (2011) arose from a nationwide sex-discrimination claim by female employees. The Court held that commonality requires a common contention capable of classwide resolution, so that determining its truth or falsity resolves an issue central to each claim in one stroke. A company-wide policy of discretion by local managers was not such a contention. The Court also held that claims for individualised monetary relief, such as backpay, may not be certified under Rule 23(b)(2). Amchem Products, Inc. v. Windsor (1997) held that a settlement-only class of asbestos claimants failed predominance and adequacy requirements, while Comcast Corp. v. Behrend (2013) requires a damages model to match the plaintiff's theory of liability. Under Phillips Petroleum Co. v. Shutts (1985), absent members can be bound without minimum contacts with the forum if they receive notice, an opportunity to opt out, and adequate representation. Smith v. Bayer Corp. (2011) held that a court's denial of certification does not bind absent members in later cases because they were not parties. TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez (2021) held that every class member must have Article III standing to recover individual damages.

The Class Action Fairness Act, 28 U.S.C. section 1332(d), gives federal courts original jurisdiction over class actions in which the aggregate amount exceeds $5 million, the class has at least 100 members, and any member is a citizen of a different state from any defendant, subject to exceptions for local controversies and home-state cases. A settlement requires court approval as fair, reasonable and adequate under Rule 23(e), and a certification decision may be appealed by permission under Rule 23(f), with a petition due within 14 days.

Worked example. Ten thousand consumers each lost 40 dollars from the same hidden fee. Damages are formulaic, common questions predominate, and (b)(3) certification is likely. If instead each driver was injured in an unrelated crash with different facts, individual issues would predominate.

lessons.title: Discovery
body: Discovery is the pretrial process by which parties obtain information from each other and from nonparties. Its purpose is to narrow disputes, avoid surprise, and promote settlement or summary adjudication. The scope is set by Rule 26(b)(1): parties may obtain discovery of any nonprivileged matter that is relevant to any party's claim or defence and proportional to the needs of the case, considering the importance of the issues, the amount in controversy, the parties' relative access to information, their resources, the importance of the discovery, and whether its burden outweighs its likely benefit. The information need not be admissible at trial to be discoverable.

The tools are distinct. Initial disclosures under Rule 26(a)(1) must be made without a request and include witnesses, documents, a computation of damages, and insurance agreements. Depositions under Rule 30 are questioning under oath, limited by default to 10 per side and one day of seven hours per deponent. Interrogatories under Rule 33 are written questions to parties, limited to 25 including discrete subparts. Requests for production under Rule 34 reach documents, electronically stored information and tangible things. Requests for admission under Rule 36 ask a party to admit facts, and unanswered requests are deemed admitted. Rule 35 allows a physical or mental examination on motion for good cause when a party has put its condition in controversy. A nonparty is reached by subpoena under Rule 45. Discovery generally cannot begin until the parties have conferred under Rule 26(f).

Privilege and work product limit discovery. Attorney-client privilege protects confidential communications made for legal advice. Upjohn Co. v. United States (1981) held that it covers communications between a corporation's employees and its counsel made to enable counsel to give legal advice, not just those of the control group. The work-product doctrine, from Hickman v. Taylor (1947) and now Rule 26(b)(3), protects documents prepared in anticipation of litigation; ordinary work product can be obtained on a showing of substantial need and inability to get the equivalent without undue hardship, while mental impressions, conclusions and opinions of counsel receive near-absolute protection. A party withholding information as privileged must describe it so that others can assess the claim, usually in a privilege log. Federal Rule of Evidence 502 provides that inadvertent disclosure does not waive privilege if reasonable steps were taken to prevent and correct it.

Enforcement is by motion. Rule 26(c) lets the court issue protective orders for good cause to protect against annoyance, embarrassment, oppression or undue burden. Rule 37(a) allows a motion to compel, and a party that loses must usually pay the reasonable expenses unless its position was substantially justified. Rule 37(b) and (c) provide sanctions for violating orders or failing to disclose, and Rule 37(e) addresses lost electronically stored information.

Worked example. In a product-liability suit, the plaintiff requests every internal email in the manufacturer's files for ten years. The manufacturer objects as disproportionate and offers emails from two relevant departments over three years. A court weighing Rule 26(b)(1) factors may narrow the request. An attorney's memo analysing the case strategy is opinion work product and not discoverable.

lessons.title: Summary Judgment and Judgment as a Matter of Law
body: Summary judgment ends a case or an issue without trial. Under Rule 56(a), the court must grant it if the movant shows that there is no genuine dispute as to any material fact and that the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. A fact is material if it could affect the outcome under governing law, and a dispute is genuine if a reasonable jury could return a verdict for the nonmoving party. The court views the evidence in the light most favourable to the nonmovant and draws reasonable inferences in that party's favour, and it does not weigh evidence or decide credibility, as Tolan v. Cotton (2014) emphasised.

The 1986 trilogy defines the burdens. Celotex Corp. v. Catrett held that a party who will not bear the burden of proof at trial may win summary judgment by pointing out the absence of evidence on an essential element of the opponent's case; it need not produce evidence negating that element. The movant who will bear the burden at trial, by contrast, must present evidence that would entitle it to a directed verdict if uncontroverted. Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc. held that the genuineness inquiry looks to the substantive evidentiary standard that applies at trial, so a plaintiff who must prove actual malice by clear and convincing evidence must produce evidence on which a jury could so find. Matsushita Electric Industrial Co. v. Zenith Radio Corp. held that when a claim is implausible, the nonmovant must come forward with more persuasive evidence than would otherwise be required. Scott v. Harris (2007) added that a court need not accept a party's account when it is blatantly contradicted by a video in the record.

Procedure matters. Rule 56(c)(1) requires each side to support factual positions by citing materials in the record or showing that the materials do not establish a dispute; an affidavit must be made on personal knowledge and set out admissible facts. Rule 56(d) allows a court to defer or deny the motion if the nonmovant shows by affidavit that it cannot yet present facts essential to its opposition. Rule 56(f) allows judgment on grounds not raised by a party only after notice and a reasonable chance to respond.

Judgment as a matter of law under Rule 50 applies during or after trial. Rule 50(a) allows a motion before the case is submitted to the jury when a reasonable jury would not have a legally sufficient evidentiary basis to find for the party. The renewed motion under Rule 50(b) must be made within 28 days after judgment and is available only if a Rule 50(a) motion was made before submission, as emphasised in Unitherm Food Systems, Inc. v. Swift-Eckrich, Inc. (2006). Reeves v. Sanderson Plumbing Products, Inc. (2000) confirms that the Rule 50 standard mirrors the summary-judgment standard. A Rule 59 motion for new trial permits a judge to set aside a verdict against the weight of the evidence, a power broader than Rule 50.

Worked example. A tenant sues a landlord for breach of the warranty of habitability. The landlord moves for summary judgment, noting that the tenant has produced no evidence of any defect. Under Celotex the landlord prevails unless the tenant points to record evidence of the defect.

lessons.title: Trial and the Jury Right
body: The Seventh Amendment provides that in suits at common law, where the value in controversy exceeds twenty dollars, the right of trial by jury shall be preserved, and that no fact tried by a jury shall be otherwise reexamined in any court of the United States except according to the rules of the common law. It applies in federal courts and has not been incorporated against the states, so a state civil jury right depends on state constitutions. Whether a claim carries a jury right depends on the historical test: whether the action is legal rather than equitable, judged by the practice of English courts in 1791, along with the nature of the remedy sought, the remedy being the more important consideration.

Several cases show the rules. When legal and equitable claims share common issues, the legal ones go to the jury first. In Beacon Theatres, Inc. v. Westover (1959), the Court held that a court could not decide an equitable claim first in a way that would deprive the party of a jury on common legal issues. Dairy Queen, Inc. v. Wood (1962) held that a claim for an accounting that was really a claim for money damages was legal and triable to a jury. Ross v. Bernhard (1970) held that issues in a shareholder derivative suit are tried to a jury if the corporation itself would have had a right. Curtis v. Loether (1974) held that a statutory claim for damages for housing discrimination is analogous to a common-law tort and carries a jury right. Tull v. United States (1987) held that the jury decides liability for civil penalties but not their amount, while Feltner v. Columbia Pictures Television, Inc. (1998) held that a party has a right to a jury determination of copyright statutory damages. Markman v. Westview Instruments, Inc. (1996) assigned patent claim construction to the judge. No jury right attaches to purely equitable relief such as an injunction or specific performance.

Jury mechanics are set by rule. Under Rule 38, a party must demand a jury in writing no later than 14 days after the last pleading directed to the issue, and a failure to do so waives the right. Under Rule 48, a jury must have at least six and no more than twelve members, and the verdict must be unanimous unless the parties stipulate otherwise. Colgrove v. Battin (1973) held that a six-person jury satisfies the Seventh Amendment. The Court held in Edmonson v. Leesville Concrete Co. (1991) that a private litigant in a civil case may not exclude jurors by race through peremptory challenges. Objections to jury instructions must be raised under Rule 51 before the jury retires.

The re-examination clause limits judicial control of the verdict. Courts may order a new trial or conditional remittitur, but may not enter additur, which the Court rejected in Dimick v. Schiedt (1935). Galloway v. United States (1943) held that directed verdicts do not violate the clause.

Worked example. A buyer sues for rescission of a contract, an equitable remedy, and alternatively for damages for fraud. The seller demands a jury. The fraud damages issues go to the jury first, and the judge is then bound by its findings on common facts when deciding the equitable claim.

lessons.title: Claim Preclusion
body: Claim preclusion, traditionally called res judicata, says that a valid final judgment on the merits bars the same parties, or those in privity with them, from relitigating the same claim. It extends both to matters that were actually litigated and to matters that could have been raised in that first action. The doctrine promotes finality, protects defendants from repeated suits, and conserves judicial resources. A plaintiff who wins is said to have merged the claim into the judgment; a defendant who wins has a bar against later suit on that claim.

The elements are usually stated as three: a final judgment on the merits by a court of competent jurisdiction; the same parties or their privies; and the same claim or cause of action. Most American courts define same claim by the transactional test of Restatement (Second) of Judgments section 24: the claim includes all rights to remedies against the defendant with respect to all or any part of the transaction or series of connected transactions out of which the action arose, regardless of the number of legal theories or remedies sought. A plaintiff injured in a collision cannot sue first for the vehicle damage and again for the injuries; both arise from one transaction. Federal Rule 13(a), which makes compulsory counterclaims arising from the same transaction mandatory, applies a similar rule to defendants.

What counts as a judgment on the merits is specific. Under Rule 41(b), a dismissal other than for lack of jurisdiction, improper venue or failure to join a party under Rule 19 operates as an adjudication on the merits unless the court says otherwise. So a dismissal for failure to state a claim, a summary judgment, a judgment after trial and a default judgment all trigger preclusion. A dismissal for lack of jurisdiction or venue does not, and a voluntary dismissal under Rule 41(a)(1) is without prejudice unless the plaintiff has previously dismissed the same claim in any court, in which case the second operates as an adjudication on the merits. Federated Department Stores, Inc. v. Moitie (1981) held that a judgment is not made less preclusive because it rests on a legal theory that a different court later rejected; litigants who do not appeal are bound.

Semtek International Inc. v. Lockheed Martin Corp. (2001) addressed which law determines the preclusive effect of a federal judgment in a diversity case. The Court held that the claim-preclusive effect is governed by federal common law, which adopts the law that would be applied by state courts in the state where the federal court sits, so a Rule 41(b) dismissal on the merits in federal court does not by itself bar a suit in another state when that state's law would permit it. The preclusive effect of a state judgment is controlled by 28 U.S.C. section 1738 and the law of the rendering state.

Worked example. Ruth sues Tom for breach of a supply contract and loses on summary judgment. She then sues Tom for fraud in inducing the same contract. Because both arise from the same transaction and the first judgment was on the merits, the second claim is barred even though she did not plead fraud the first time.

lessons.title: Issue Preclusion
body: Issue preclusion, also called collateral estoppel, bars relitigation of an issue of fact or law that was actually litigated and determined by a valid final judgment, when the determination was essential to the judgment. Unlike claim preclusion, it applies even if the second case is about a different claim, and it requires that the issue be identical and the party against whom it is asserted have had a full and fair opportunity to litigate it. An issue that was settled, not decided, or admitted in a default is generally not actually litigated. A finding that was not necessary to the outcome, such as dicta, does not preclude, and when a judgment rests on two independent alternative grounds, courts differ on whether either is preclusive.

Historically, estoppel required mutuality: only a party who could have been bound by the first judgment could invoke it. Courts abandoned the requirement in many settings. Blonder-Tongue Laboratories, Inc. v. University of Illinois Foundation (1971) allowed a defendant to use defensively a prior judgment holding a patent invalid against a patentee who had litigated and lost. Parklane Hosiery Co. v. Shore (1979) approved offensive nonmutual collateral estoppel in federal court, where a plaintiff uses a prior judgment against a defendant, in that case an SEC injunction suit finding the proxy statement misleading, to prevent relitigation by a later private plaintiff. The Court gave trial courts discretion to refuse it when the plaintiff could easily have joined the earlier action, so avoiding a wait-and-see approach; when the defendant had little incentive to defend vigorously the earlier suit; when the judgment was inconsistent with another prior judgment; or when procedural opportunities in the second suit would be unavailable in the first, such as a jury trial. The Seventh Amendment objection was rejected.

Nonparties are generally not bound by a judgment, because everyone is entitled to their own day in court. Taylor v. Sturgell (2008) rejected a broad theory of virtual representation and listed the recognised exceptions: agreement, preexisting substantive legal relationships, adequate representation by a party with notice, control of the litigation by the nonparty, assumption of control as a proxy, and special statutory schemes such as bankruptcy and probate. Montana v. United States (1979) applied preclusion to the United States when it controlled an earlier state-court suit, and the principle that the government may be bound when it was a participant.

Federal courts must give state-court judgments the same preclusive effect they would receive in the courts of the rendering state, by 28 U.S.C. section 1738 and the Full Faith and Credit Clause, which applies in many contexts. Preclusion is an affirmative defence under Rule 8(c) and is waived if not pleaded.

Worked example. In a bench trial, a court finds that a tire manufacturer knew its tire design was defective. Later plaintiffs injured by the same tire sue the manufacturer. Under Parklane, a later plaintiff may argue that the manufacturer cannot relitigate the finding, but the court may refuse if the manufacturer had little reason to fight the first case because of a small amount at stake.

lessons.title: Appeals and Post-Judgment Relief
body: Federal appellate review is statutory. Under 28 U.S.C. section 1291, the courts of appeals have jurisdiction over appeals from all final decisions of the district courts. A final decision is one that ends the litigation on the merits and leaves nothing for the court to do but execute the judgment. The rule avoids piecemeal appeals, delay and wasted effort, and it means that a party must usually wait until the end of the case to challenge earlier rulings. A party cannot manufacture finality by voluntarily dismissing remaining claims to obtain review of an adverse ruling, a tactic rejected in Microsoft Corp. v. Baker (2017) in the class certification context.

There are exceptions. Under Rule 54(b), a court may direct entry of final judgment as to fewer than all claims or parties if it expressly determines there is no just reason for delay. Under section 1292(a)(1), orders granting, refusing or modifying injunctions are immediately appealable. Under section 1292(b), a district judge may certify an order that involves a controlling question of law as to which there is substantial ground for difference of opinion and whose immediate appeal may materially advance the litigation, but the court of appeals must also agree to hear it, and the application is due within ten days of the certification. Under the collateral order doctrine of Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan Corp. (1949), a small class of orders that conclusively determine a disputed question, resolve an important issue completely separate from the merits, and are effectively unreviewable after final judgment can be appealed immediately; the Court interprets the class narrowly, as in Mohawk Industries, Inc. v. Carpenter (2009), which held that orders requiring disclosure of material claimed to be privileged are not within it. Denial of qualified immunity to a government official, based on a question of law, is an example that is within it. Class certification orders may be appealed by permission under Rule 23(f). Extraordinary relief by writ of mandamus is available only in exceptional circumstances.

Timing is jurisdictional. Under Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 4(a)(1)(A), the notice of appeal in a civil case is due within 30 days after entry of the judgment, and 60 days when the United States is a party. Certain timely post-judgment motions, such as a Rule 59(e) motion to alter or amend the judgment filed within 28 days, suspend the running of the period.

The standard of review depends on the type of ruling. Appellate courts decide questions of law de novo. Findings of fact by a judge are reviewed for clear error under Rule 52(a)(6), and Anderson v. City of Bessemer City (1985) explains that a finding is not clearly erroneous merely because the court of appeals would have weighed the evidence differently. Discretionary rulings such as discovery orders and decisions on motions to amend are reviewed for abuse of discretion. Errors that do not affect substantial rights are harmless under Rule 61.

Rule 60(b) provides relief from a final judgment for mistake, newly discovered evidence that could not have been found in time, fraud, a void judgment, a satisfied judgment, or any other reason justifying relief. Motions based on mistake, new evidence or fraud must be made within a reasonable time and no more than one year after entry.

Worked example. A judge grants summary judgment against one of three defendants. The plaintiff cannot appeal immediately unless the judge enters a Rule 54(b) judgment with an express no-just-reason-for-delay finding; otherwise the ruling is reviewable only after the whole case ends.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the jurisdiction of the federal district courts?
choices: They hold the same broad authority as state trial courts but must defer to a state court that first took jurisdiction of the dispute
They may hear any civil dispute whose parties consent in writing to federal jurisdiction before the complaint is filed
They have only the power granted by Article III and by Congress, and the party invoking federal jurisdiction bears the burden of showing it exists
They have general jurisdiction over every civil dispute, exactly like state trial courts, unless a state constitution expressly reserves the matter to its own courts

questions.prompt: Both parties to a federal contract suit between citizens of one state spend a year in discovery without objecting to jurisdiction. The claim is purely state law. What should happen when the defect is noticed?
choices: The court may proceed, because a year of participation without objection ratifies the court's authority over the dispute
The court should transfer the case to another federal district, because the defect is a venue problem curable by transfer
The court may keep the case if the plaintiff files an amended complaint adding a request for declaratory relief
The court must dismiss, because parties cannot confer subject-matter jurisdiction by consent, waiver or silence

questions.prompt: What limit does the Rules Enabling Act place on the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure?
choices: The Rules may not abridge, enlarge or modify any substantive right
The Rules may not apply to any case that is based on state law rather than federal law
The Rules must be re-enacted by each state legislature before a federal court can apply them within that state
The Rules may regulate only the trial stage and may not govern pleading, discovery or motions practice

questions.prompt: Alvarez, a citizen of Nevada, sues Bolt Co., also a Nevada citizen, in federal court on a state-law negligence claim for $400,000. Bolt answers and litigates for a year. On appeal after a verdict for Alvarez, Bolt first argues lack of jurisdiction. What is the most likely result?
choices: The case is remanded for transfer to a Nevada state court, which must accept the federal verdict as a binding judgment
The judgment is vacated and the case dismissed, because lack of subject-matter jurisdiction can be raised at any time, even for the first time on appeal
The judgment stands, because Bolt waived the objection by answering the complaint without raising jurisdiction in its first Rule 12 response, so the issue was forfeited before trial
The judgment stands, because the amount in controversy exceeds the statutory threshold and that alone supports the exercise of federal power

questions.prompt: A plaintiff files a diversity case in federal court. The defendant moves to dismiss both for lack of personal jurisdiction and, in the alternative, for failure to state a claim. The court has doubts about its subject-matter jurisdiction but is confident the complaint is weak on the merits. Under Steel Co., what should the court do first?
choices: Assume jurisdiction for the sake of argument and rule on the strongest merits ground the defendant raised
Require the defendant to file an answer so the jurisdictional facts can be developed through discovery
Resolve its subject-matter jurisdiction before ruling on the merits of the complaint
Dismiss the complaint on the merits, since a plainly meritless claim can be rejected without deciding jurisdiction

questions.prompt: Under the well-pleaded complaint rule, where must the federal question appear to support section 1331 jurisdiction?
choices: In the court's own review of the whole record after discovery has revealed the contested legal issues
In the plaintiff's own properly pleaded complaint, not in an anticipated defence
In the defendant's answer, because the defendant controls which defences are raised
In either party's pleading, because any federal issue in the case suffices to arise under federal law

questions.prompt: Lena sues a bank in state court for breach of a loan contract under state law. The bank wants to argue federal preemption. May it remove the case on that basis alone?
choices: No, because preemption is a defence and does not appear in the well-pleaded complaint
Yes, because any case in which federal law will decide the outcome may be removed to federal court
Yes, because preemption claims always arise under federal law within the meaning of section 1331
No, because contract disputes can never be removed from state court under any jurisdictional statute

questions.prompt: Which feature is part of the Grable test for state-law claims that raise a federal issue?
choices: The federal issue must be mentioned anywhere in the complaint, even if the state-law claim could succeed without resolving it, so long as the defendant anticipates a federal defence
The federal statute involved must provide a private cause of action, or jurisdiction is always denied
The state-law claim must have been preempted by a federal statute that fully occupies the field of regulation
The federal issue must be necessary to the claim, actually disputed and substantial, and resolvable without upsetting the federal-state balance

questions.prompt: Orla, a former client, sues her patent lawyer in state court for malpractice, alleging he lost an earlier patent case through negligence. Resolving the malpractice claim would require deciding a federal patent question as a hypothetical. The lawyer removes. Under Gunn v. Minton, the federal court should
choices: keep the case, because the lawyer is the defendant and may remove whenever a federal defence appears
remand only if Orla amends to drop the patent references, since the court looks at the later pleadings
remand, because the federal issue is a hypothetical "case within a case" that would not alter the patent outcome and is not substantial to the federal system
keep the case, because patent law is exclusively federal and any claim touching patents arises under federal law, including malpractice claims about a lost patent suit

questions.prompt: A state-law quiet-title suit turns entirely on whether the Internal Revenue Service gave notice satisfying a federal statute before seizing property. The federal issue is the only disputed question, it matters to the government, and hearing it in federal court would open the door to few state-law cases. What is the best conclusion under Grable?
choices: Federal jurisdiction is lacking, because the property is located in a state court's territory and quiet title is always local
Federal jurisdiction exists, because the federal issue is disputed, substantial and capable of being heard without disturbing the balance
Federal jurisdiction is lacking, because the plaintiff pleaded only state law and the statute gives no private damages right
Federal jurisdiction exists only if the parties are diverse and over $75,000, because federal issues embedded in state-law claims do not count under section 1331

questions.prompt: What does the complete diversity rule require?
choices: No plaintiff may share state citizenship with any defendant
At least one plaintiff and at least one defendant must be citizens of different states
Each plaintiff must be a citizen of a state different from the state where the claim arose
The majority of the parties on each side must be citizens of different states from the other side

questions.prompt: Orion Corp. is incorporated in Delaware and its executives direct and control its business from headquarters in Texas. Of what states is Orion a citizen for diversity purposes?
choices: Every state in which Orion owns property or sells goods
Delaware and Texas
Delaware only, because the state of incorporation is the sole controlling factor
Texas only, because the nerve center replaces the state of incorporation

questions.prompt: A single plaintiff asserts two unrelated contract claims of $50,000 each against one defendant. Both claims rest on state law and the parties are diverse. What is the amount-in-controversy result?
choices: Only the claim the plaintiff chooses first can proceed in federal court, and the second must be filed separately
The court must apply the legal certainty test to each claim separately and dismiss any claim under the threshold
The claims may be aggregated, so the amount exceeds $75,000 and diversity jurisdiction is available
The claims may not be aggregated because they are unrelated, so jurisdiction fails for both claims

questions.prompt: Priya, domiciled in Texas, sues Marcus, domiciled in Oklahoma, and Delta LLC, whose three members are citizens of Oklahoma, Texas and Ohio, for $200,000 on a state contract. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: Complete diversity exists, because Delta LLC was organised under one state's law and takes that state's citizenship alone
Complete diversity exists, because only the citizenship of Marcus, an individual defendant, counts when entities are co-defendants
Complete diversity is lacking only if Delta LLC's principal place of business is in Texas, because LLCs are treated like corporations under section 1332(c)(1)
Complete diversity is lacking, because Delta LLC is treated as a citizen of every state of which any member is a citizen, including Texas

questions.prompt: Waleed, a United States citizen domiciled permanently in France, sues Gerald, a citizen of New York, on a state contract claim for $300,000 in federal court. The best analysis is that
choices: diversity is lacking, because a United States citizen domiciled abroad is neither a citizen of a state nor an alien
diversity exists, because Waleed is a United States citizen and Gerald is a New York citizen, and the amount in controversy exceeds the statutory threshold
diversity exists under the alienage clause, because Waleed lives in a foreign country
diversity is available only if Waleed can show he last lived in a state different from New York

questions.prompt: According to United Mine Workers v. Gibbs, claims are part of the same constitutional case for supplemental jurisdiction when they
choices: are filed on the same day in the same courthouse
are governed by the same state statute of limitations
derive from a common nucleus of operative fact
involve the same attorneys and the same witnesses

questions.prompt: A plaintiff files in a Georgia state court against a Georgia citizen, and the plaintiff is from Florida, with $500,000 at stake on a state claim. May the defendant remove?
choices: Yes, but only after the plaintiff consents in writing to removal within thirty days of service
No, because diversity cases may never be removed from state to federal court
No, because the forum-defendant rule bars removal in a diversity case by a defendant who is a citizen of the forum state
Yes, because complete diversity and the amount in controversy are satisfied, which is all that section 1441 requires for removal of a state-court suit

questions.prompt: In Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Allapattah Services, Inc., what did the Court hold about plaintiffs whose claims are below the amount-in-controversy threshold?
choices: Supplemental jurisdiction also allows plaintiffs who lack complete diversity to proceed as long as one is diverse
If complete diversity exists and one plaintiff meets the threshold, section 1367 allows jurisdiction over other plaintiffs' smaller claims
Plaintiffs whose claims are under the threshold may never join an action that includes a plaintiff over the threshold, because each plaintiff must independently satisfy it
The smaller claims may be heard only if the court first aggregates all plaintiffs' claims into a single total

questions.prompt: Chen, a Florida citizen, sues Dorn, a Georgia citizen, in federal court for $200,000. Dorn impleads Eaton, a Florida citizen, under Rule 14, for indemnity. Chen then amends to assert a state claim directly against Eaton. What is the likely result as to Chen's claim against Eaton?
